rv.q: There's something deeply satisfying about this little play.
And what a quietly satisfying, touching pleasure this production, staged by Tony-winning director Michael Grandage (“Red”), turns out to be.

In Michael Grandage's gentle, churning dream of a revival of Eugene O'Neill's 'Hughie'...Erie is portrayed by that excellent actor Forest Whitaker, in a transfixing yet modest Broadway debut. Mr. Whitaker provides all the anchoring physical detail that you might expect from his meticulously observed screen performances...Yet as you watch Mr.
All of this registers in the countenance of a terrific American actor, who’s found a comfortable home on the stage of the Booth, when the man he plays never truly can.
Nothing significant happens in “Hughie” except theatre—and the creative lives of its actors.
Whitaker's hangdog vulnerability makes it tough to believe in Erie's better days — and besides, there's no pretending that 'Hughie' is much more than a warm-up for 'Iceman.'
We are desperate to believe in what is happening on stage even when it disappoints.
Unusually for an O’Neill play and perhaps even more unusual for a play about a gambler, the dramatic stakes are perilously low.

Whitaker must make sure that, unlike Eerie's audience of the lone night clerk (played by Frank Wood, perfecting an eyes-open narcolepsy), we are not bored to stupefaction. Instead, he must be sufficiently magnetic and compelling in his patter that we, the real audience, never want him to shut up...
To use gambling lingo, the revival is a king short of a royal flush.
Stars are aligning on stage this week — though in most cases, you'd better stay out of their orbit.
But a huge set for a small play is usually compensating for something.
I’m sorry to say that Forest Whitaker has failed to beat the odds in Eugene O’Neill’s “Hughie.”
Whitaker is out of his depth and has a very hesitant stage range.

There’s only so much a shorter show like this can answer — I was left wanting to know more about both Erie and the night clerk after I left for the night — but it’s still a hotel stay you won’t regret.
Whitaker delivers a most endearing Erie, right down to the nervous giggle he adds to punctuate the character’s otherwise bottomless despair.
Whitaker makes his character worthy of compassion.
Indeed, this short work is a wonderful character study and an affecting portrait of grief.
I’d wager that Whitaker’s performance will evolve in the weeks ahead, but for the moment he’s throwing snake eyes.
Producing 'Hughie' as a stand-alone drama on Broadway is pretty questionable.
When O'Neill once said about the play that it was written more to be read than staged, he might have added "and more to be mourned than mounted."
“It’s a brave, if odd, choice for a Broadway debut, this meager work that reads better than it plays…The biggest miscue of Michael Grandage’s production is that Erie seems to believe his bullshit.
But that's about all this undercooked, altogether listless production has going for it.
But Whitaker doesn't, so "Hughie" craps out.
Whereas Long Day’s Journey and Iceman dwell ruefully in gloom for upwards of four and five hours, Hughie gives us only one hour of two people making small talk in a hotel lobby.
Whitaker's performance was pure magic.
This production of Hughie vividly fulfills O’Neill’s intentions with its inspired physical representation and engrossing performances.
As a playwright, O’Neill aged like few others and published his best work at the end of his career.

Adam Cork’s brooding original music and sound design and Neil Austin’s muted and affecting lighting design also play a major part in the play’s success, creating a pervasive, ominous sense of dread and foreboding.
Overall, the play is a simple but poignant rumination on the lies we have to tell each other -- and tell ourselves -- to make our way in the world.
To be transported to this bit of old New York, and to spend some time with one of its denizens, is a nice treat but still may not feel like a completely fulfilling evening of theater.
This is really a shame, for while by no means perfect, this production of “Hughie” is still very much worth a look.
Hughie, no matter how beautifully produced, performed, directed, remains a minor note.

"Whitaker plays a very generalized Erie Smith almost entirely on one note, a genial rube who thinks he’s wise, with a very generalized need to talk, never quite making the Broadway patois of the day fully his own.
Hughie is more effective as a work of literature – a reading experience – than a star vehicle, at least based on the current production of it.
In the end, by the sheer brevity of the play, its repetitive nature, and Whitaker’s semi-successful star turn, I believe we’ve all been shortchanged.
Sadly, Whitaker's performance is far too undistinguished to believe his Erie would merit such status.
Considering there is no plot or point to this play, the bravado has to be an essential part of the show, for without it the show becomes a big snooze.
Unfortunately Erie could be describing Michael Grandage’s lifeless production as well as Christopher Oram’s appropriately funereal set.

“This is a two person show that lasts 60 minutes…Forest Whitaker enters the elegantly designed set and he rambles for 60 minutes. Then the show ends. This is all. I didn't have a clue why we were watching him, why he was there, and frankly was bored and disgusted at his pointless babbling. Dumb, Expensive, Meaningless.
